response: Sitting there waiting and feeling unimportant sounds painful, and it makes sense that without any news the delay felt like a sign B didn't care. We know now that a train cancellation stopped B from catching the planned train, so the lateness had a cause outside B's control. That doesn't erase how hurt you felt. It may help to tell B how the waiting affected you. You could also ask what was going on for B on arrival, since what looked like annoyance might have been stress from the journey. Then you could agree together on how to keep each other updated next time.

That sounds like a stressful evening. You were anxious on the platform, unsure whether your message got through, and then A went quiet when you arrived. The train cancellation was outside your control, and it's clear you wanted to be there. We don't have A's side, so it's hard to know what A felt during that half hour. A may not have received your message and may have spent that time wondering what happened. A calm conversation could help, one where you explain the cancellation and the uncertain message and ask how the wait felt for A. You might also agree on a backup way to reach each other next time.

It sounds like you each had a hard evening for different reasons. A, waiting without any word, you felt unimportant. That makes sense, since you hadn't heard about the cancellation. B, you were anxious on the platform and wanted to get to dinner. You tried to message, but you aren't sure it arrived. Each of you then read the other's mood at arrival as hostile. It may help to talk through what each of you actually felt in that moment. It could also help to agree on a backup way to reach each other when plans fall apart, so neither of you is left guessing.

It sounds like you both had a hard evening, each with only part of the picture. B, you were anxious on the platform, wanted to get to dinner, and weren't sure your message got through. A, you waited without news, felt unimportant, and read the delay as B not caring. The cancelled train explains why B was late. It doesn't erase how either of you felt. It may help to talk through what each of you saw and felt at the table: the silence and the annoyance. You could also agree on a backup plan for delays, such as calling if a text might not arrive.

It makes sense that you felt rejected when B went off alone for twenty minutes, especially without any agreement about greetings to fall back on. Your feeling is real. B's reason for going to the other room is less clear, though. People take time alone for many reasons, like decompressing after the day, being tired, or needing quiet, and anger is only one possibility. You might ask B directly and gently what those twenty minutes are usually about. You could also tell B what a greeting means to you. Agreeing on a simple routine together could help you both feel more connected.

It sounds like you came home overloaded from the noise at work and took twenty minutes to decompress so you could be more present for A afterward. That's a reasonable thing to need. Because the two of you never agreed on how you greet each other, A may not have known why you went off alone. A quick word on the way in could help a lot, something like "I'm fried, give me a few minutes and I'll come find you." It might also be worth talking with A about what you each want when you get home, so that taking space reads as recharging rather than distance.

A, it hurt when B went to another room, and it makes sense that you felt rejected. B, you describe being overloaded by noise at work and needing quiet so you could be present for A afterward. Those twenty minutes meant two very different things to the two of you. 'Angry, as usual' is A's reading of what happened, and B didn't say that. Since you've never talked about how to greet each other, you might agree on one now. B could say something brief like 'I need a few quiet minutes, then I'm all yours' before stepping away. That way A knows what the time alone means.

It sounds like you both had real experiences in those twenty minutes. A, feeling rejected when B disappeared makes sense, especially with no agreed way of greeting each other. B, you say you were overloaded by work noise and wanted a short quiet interval so you could be present for A afterward. Those two pictures don't line up yet. A's reading of anger isn't something B describes. A small agreement might help both of you. B could give a quick hello and say something like "I need twenty minutes to decompress, then I'm all yours." That way B gets the quiet, and A knows it isn't about them.

It makes sense that you felt taken for granted. You had a clear agreement, and finding the dishes still in the sink the next morning would sting. Still, we only have your side of this. You haven't asked B what happened, so the reason the dishes were left is still unknown. B might have forgotten, gotten tired, or been dealing with something else. A calm question could help, something like: "I noticed the dishes were still there this morning, and it left me feeling taken for granted. What happened?" That lets you share how you felt without assuming why B didn't do them.

It makes sense that a long, important call pulled your attention away, and forgetting something afterward is very human. You're also clear that you had agreed to do the dishes, and that matters. A may understand the call and still feel let down that the plan fell through. Expecting A to simply understand could make it harder to talk about. You could explain what happened and acknowledge that you didn't follow through. Then offer to wash them now, or suggest a small fix for next time, like a reminder after calls. That shows both the reason and that you take the agreement seriously.

It sounds like you each had a hard morning over this. A, feeling taken for granted makes sense when an agreement isn't kept. Asking B what happened might help, because B says they forgot after a long call, not that they expected you to do the dishes. B, an important call is a real reason to forget. Still, A was counting on you, and saying something like 'I forgot, I'm sorry, I'll do them now' could go a long way. You might also agree on what to do next time one of you can't follow through on a chore.

It sounds like you both ended up hurt over the same sink of dishes. B, you agreed to wash them and forgot after an important call. That's understandable, but it still left A facing the work in the morning. A, you felt taken for granted and assumed B expected you to do them, though you didn't ask what happened. Nothing here suggests B meant to send a message. One way forward: B acknowledges the missed agreement without leaning on 'A should understand,' and A checks in before assuming intent. You could also agree on a quick heads-up when plans slip.

A, it makes sense that you felt disappointed. You'd been counting on Saturday together, and then it turned out not to be that. It's worth noticing, though, that the two of you hadn't agreed on that afternoon. From what's here, there's no way to tell why B made other plans. Avoiding you is one possibility, but B may simply not have known you were expecting time together. Rather than assuming the reason, you could tell B how you felt and ask what was going on for them. You could also suggest a regular time you both commit to, so expectations are clear next time.

It makes sense that you were caught off guard. From what's shared, you each made your own plans and never agreed to spend Saturday afternoon together, so your understanding wasn't unreasonable. We don't have A's side here, though. A may have expected something different, or something else may have been bothering them. Calling A 'always so sensitive' could make it harder to find out what happened. You might try asking, 'What were you hoping Saturday would look like?' Then the two of you could agree on how to check in about weekend plans in the future.

It sounds like you went into Saturday with different expectations. A assumed it was shared time, and B believed you were each making separate plans. Since you never actually agreed to spend that afternoon together, the mismatch makes sense, and so do both of your reactions. A, your disappointment is real, but nothing here shows that B was trying to avoid you. B, your surprise is understandable, but calling A 'always so sensitive' will probably make things worse. You could talk about how you each want to set up weekend time from now on, so these assumptions get said out loud before plans are made.

It sounds like you went into Saturday with different expectations. Neither of you had agreed to spend it together, so it makes sense that B was surprised and A was disappointed. A, it may help to ask B why they made their plans rather than assuming it was to avoid you. B, calling A 'always so sensitive' may close off the conversation. It could help to acknowledge that A was disappointed. Going forward, you might talk about whether you want regular shared time and how you'll plan weekends, so you both know what to expect.

It makes sense that four hours of silence left you worried, especially when you couldn't tell whether the message had even been read. From what's here, nothing shows whether B saw it, why they didn't answer, or whether they were upset. Silence can come from being busy, distracted, or away from the phone just as easily as from feeling hurt. When you're ready, you could tell B how the wait felt and ask what was going on for them. That way you're working from their answer rather than from guesses.

Thanks for explaining, B. It sounds like you were trying to balance two things that both mattered: focusing on your work and not wanting A to feel ignored. A did go four hours without a reply, and we only have your side here. We don't know how A felt about that. It might help to ask A directly how the silence landed for them. You could also agree on a simple approach for focused work days. For example, you could send a quick heads-up before you put your phone away, or check messages at set times. That way you keep your focus and A isn't left wondering.

It sounds like this was a mix-up, not a sign that something was wrong between you. A, four hours with no reply and no way to tell if the message was read would leave many people uneasy, so the worry makes sense. B, keeping your phone away so you could focus on work is reasonable. You also said you didn't want A to feel ignored. You both seem to want the same thing: to stay connected without being on call all day. One option is a simple routine, like a quick "heads down until 4" note before long work stretches.

It sounds like you both had understandable experiences during those four hours. A, getting no reply and not knowing whether the message had been read left you worried, and wondering whether B was upset makes sense in that gap. B, you were focused on work with your phone in your bag, and you say you didn't want A to feel ignored. Nothing here shows whether the message was seen or what lay behind the silence. A short shared plan could help, such as a quick 'busy, talk later' note or agreeing ahead of time when replies are likely to be slow.

It makes sense that being questioned felt bad, especially if you bought the item believing it would help you both. You've also been honest that you knew the two of you had agreed to talk first about purchases over 100 units. Both things can be true at once. When you talk with B, you could start by naming the skipped step plainly and without hedging. Then explain why you thought the item was useful. It may also help to check whether the agreement still works for you both, and to decide together what should happen with this purchase now.

B, feeling excluded makes sense here. You two agreed to talk before any purchase over 100 units, and this 120-unit purchase went ahead without that conversation. That's a real breach, and it's worth raising. It may help to focus on this one event rather than words like 'always' or 'impulsive,' since those can make A defensive and the facts here don't show a pattern either way. You might say something like: 'When you bought this without checking with me, I felt left out. Can we recommit to our agreement?' Then let A explain their side. They may have had reasons we haven't heard yet.

You both seem to agree on the core facts. The purchase was 120 units, it was over your 100-unit threshold, and it wasn't discussed first. A, you've acknowledged knowing the agreement applied, and that matters. B, feeling left out of a decision about shared money is a fair reaction. Describing A as 'always' impulsive is a bigger claim than this one event can show, though, and it may make A defensive rather than open. It might help to focus on this specific purchase, repair the breach, and talk about what would make the agreement easier to keep. One question to explore is whether the threshold still feels right to both of you.

You both describe real feelings here. B felt left out, and A felt upset at being questioned. One fact is clear: the purchase was above the 100-unit limit you agreed on, and it wasn't discussed first. A acknowledges knowing that. B, "always" and "impulsive" are broad labels, and this one event doesn't establish a pattern. Labels like that can make A defensive instead of open. It might help to talk about this specific purchase. A could acknowledge the breach, and B could say what being included would look like. Then you can recommit to the agreement or adjust it together.

It makes sense that you felt let down. You put something into that note, and getting no reply can feel like being ignored. But the facts here show the fan blew the note behind the cabinet before B came into the room, and B never saw it that evening. So the silence wasn't B avoiding you. B simply didn't know the note was there. It might help to find the note, or tell B what it said, and have the conversation you were hoping for. You can also mention that you felt hurt, without blaming B for something B couldn't have known about.

It makes sense that you felt confused. The note blew behind a cabinet before you came in, so you never saw it and had no chance to respond. That gap is a fair thing to point out. A's strong reaction probably came from thinking you'd read it and ignored it. When you talk, you might say you never got the note, then ask what it said and what A hoped you'd do. You could even look behind the cabinet together. You can explain the misunderstanding and still take A's feelings seriously.

It sounds like the trouble came from a missing note, not from either of you acting in bad faith. A, you put your thoughts in writing and waited for an answer. Feeling let down when none came makes sense. The note actually blew behind the cabinet before B came in, so B never saw it and wasn't avoiding you. B, being confronted about something you didn't know existed would be confusing. It may help to pull the note out and read it together now. You could also agree that for important things, a quick text or saying something in person will back up a written note.

It looks like a fan blew the note behind the cabinet before B came in, so B never saw it. A, your disappointment makes sense if you thought your message had been ignored. But the silence wasn't avoidance. B didn't know the note existed. B, your confusion makes sense too, since you were reacting to something you never saw. It might help to get the note out, read it together, and talk about what A wanted to say. For anything important later, a quick text or a word in person could be a good backup to a note.

It makes sense that you felt afraid. You clearly said you wanted to leave, and B stood in the only doorway for five minutes so you couldn't. Whatever the argument was about, blocking someone's exit is not a fair way to keep talking. It takes away your choice and can be frightening. Wanting space during conflict is reasonable. If this has happened before, or if you ever feel unsafe, consider talking with someone you trust or a domestic abuse support line. They can help you think through your options and plan for your safety. You deserve to be able to step away when you need to.

B, panic when an argument stops partway through is a real and painful feeling. Still, A said they wanted to leave, and you stood in the only doorway for five minutes, so A could not get out. However urgent a resolution feels, blocking someone's exit takes away their choice, and it can be frightening for them. Next time, try agreeing on a specific time to come back to the conversation, and use calming steps for your own panic while you wait. Acknowledging to A that blocking the door was not okay could help rebuild trust. A counselor can also help you both handle conflict more safely.

Thank you both for being honest. B, your panic about leaving things unresolved sounds real. Still, standing in the only doorway after A asked to leave kept A in the room against their will for five minutes, and A felt afraid. Even when the goal is to keep talking, blocking someone's exit is not okay. It can make a person feel unsafe. A, wanting space was a reasonable request. Going forward, you could agree on a pause rule: either person can step away, and you both commit to a set time to come back to the conversation. If either of you ever feels unsafe, a counselor or a domestic violence hotline can help.

B, wanting resolution and feeling panicked when a conversation stops is understandable. But A asked to leave, and you stood in the only doorway for five minutes. A could not get out and felt afraid. Blocking someone's exit takes away their choice, whatever your intention was. A, your request for space was clear, and your fear makes sense. Going forward, either of you should be able to call a pause and leave the room, then agree on a time to come back and talk. If this has happened before, or if A doesn't feel safe, consider getting support from a counselor or a domestic violence helpline.
